name: Xinomavro

lines.s10: Xinomavro is the pale, sharp red of northern Greece, with sour cherry, sun dried tomato and black olive on a firm grip.
lines.s20: Xinomavro is the red grape of Naoussa and Amyndeon in northern Greece, often set beside Barolo for its grip. It pours pale and turns to brick early, with sour cherry, sun dried tomato and black olive over high acidity and firm tannin.
lines.s45: Xinomavro belongs to northern Greece, to Naoussa on the slopes of Mount Vermio and to the cold plateau of Amyndeon. It looks pale and turns to brick early. It tastes of sour cherry, sun dried tomato and black olive, over very high acidity and a firm, drying tannin. The old cellars age it for years in large old casks, while newer ones pick a little earlier and handle it more gently. Set it beside roast lamb, a tomato rich braise or wild mushrooms. In Greek the name means acid black: true of the acid, though not of the colour.
lines.sale: Xinomavro gives a guest who loves Barolo something new to explore: the same pale colour and grip, with tomato and olive in place of tar. Decant the Naoussa and set it beside anything slow cooked with tomato.

glass.lead: Sour cherry, sun dried tomato and black olive in a pale garnet glass, over very high acidity and a firm, drying tannin.

ladder.where: The Amyndeon plateau, by the lakes of Western Macedonia
Naoussa, on the eastern slopes of Mount Vermio
Goumenissa above the Axios plain, and Rapsani on Olympus

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity high, tannin high and drying, alcohol medium plus, body medium; pale garnet, turning to brick early.

home.home: Northern Greece. Naoussa, on the eastern slopes of Mount Vermio, is Xinomavro alone and red only. Amyndeon, on a colder plateau, makes it red, rosé and sparkling. Goumenissa blends it with Negoska, and Rapsani on Olympus with Krassato and Stavroto.
home.abroad: It barely travels: North Macedonia, over the border, grows some, and small new vineyards have appeared in Australia and China.

service.temp: 61 to 64 degrees Fahrenheit, 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; a young, modern Naoussa a touch cooler.
service.glass: A wide Burgundy bowl, as for Nebbiolo, to gather the perfume.
service.decant: Decant a young Naoussa after a taste; an old Grande Reserve gently, off its sediment.
service.age: Ten years and more for Naoussa Reserve and Grande Reserve; a young, modern bottle within five.

labels.means: Xinomavro alone, red only, from the eastern slopes of Mount Vermio; a PDO since 1971.
Xinomavro alone from a cold lakeside plateau, as red, rosé or sparkling rosé.
Xinomavro with at least 20 per cent Negoska, a local grape that softens and deepens it.

Greece's national ageing terms; a Grande Reserve spends at least four years in cask and bottle.

guest.a: Acid black, in Greek. The acid is true to the name; the black is not, since the wine is pale and turns to brick early.

guest.q: Why do people compare it with Barolo?
guest.a: Both are pale, high in acidity and firm in tannin, and both age for decades. Xinomavro tastes of sun dried tomato and black olive where Nebbiolo has tar and roses.
Amyndeon's, from a colder plateau: paler and fresher, and also made as a dry rosé and a sparkling rosé.

compare.tell: Nebbiolo has rose petal and tar; Xinomavro shares the pale colour, acidity and grip but brings sun dried tomato, black olive and bay leaf.
Agiorgitiko, from Nemea in the south, is deeper in colour, softer and plusher; Xinomavro is pale, sharper and more tannic, with sun dried tomato and black olive.
Sangiovese has dried oregano and a gentler tannin; Xinomavro is paler and grips harder, with sun dried tomato and black olive.

cards.front: Xinomavro: what does the name mean, and where is it at home?
cards.back: Acid black, in Greek. Its home is Macedonia in northern Greece, at Naoussa, Amyndeon and Goumenissa, with Rapsani on Mount Olympus in Thessaly.

cards.front: Xinomavro's four appellations: which grapes must each of them hold?
cards.back: Naoussa, Xinomavro alone, red only. Amyndeon, alone, as red, rosé or sparkling. Goumenissa, with at least 20 per cent Negoska. Rapsani, with Krassato and Stavroto in equal parts.

cards.front: Xinomavro blind: which mix of colour, structure and aroma gives it away?
cards.back: Pale garnet turning to brick early, very high acidity and firm tannin, with sour cherry, sun dried tomato and black olive.

questions.q: A red poured blind is pale garnet with a brick rim, with sour cherry, sun dried tomato and black olive over searing acidity and firm tannin. Which grape is it?
questions.exp: Sun dried tomato and black olive on a pale, high acid, tannic frame mark Xinomavro. Nebbiolo, the nearest miss, shares the colour and the grip but brings tar and rose petal instead.

questions.q: A guest wants a dry Greek rosé made from Xinomavro under a protected appellation. Which name do you look for?
questions.exp: Amyndeon allows Xinomavro as red, rosé and sparkling rosé. Naoussa, the nearest miss, is Xinomavro too but red only; a rosé from its slopes is a regional PGI wine.

questions.q: A guest asks why the Goumenissa on the list is darker and softer than the Naoussa beside it, though both hold Xinomavro. What is the reason?
opts: It must hold at least 20 per cent Negoska
It is aged in new American oak
It is made from dried grapes
It is grown on a cold lakeside plateau
questions.exp: Goumenissa blends Xinomavro with at least a fifth of Negoska, which brings colour, alcohol and soft tannin. A cold lakeside plateau, the nearest miss, describes Amyndeon, whose wine is paler still.

report: Mode home, as the plan fixes it. Nothing contradicts TASTE.world old.

The four appellations and their rules (Naoussa Xinomavro alone and red only, of 1971; Amyndeon alone with rosé and sparkling rosé, of 1972; Goumenissa with at least 20 per cent Negoska, of 1979; Rapsani with Krassato and Stavroto in equal parts), the name as acid black, the early brick rim, the traditional large old casks against the modern gentler school, Grande Reserve at four years in cask and bottle, service at 16 to 18 degrees with a decant, and lamb, game birds, mushrooms and tomato braises all stand on the Codex's Naoussa, Amyndeon, Goumenissa and Rapsani records; sun dried tomato, black olive, laurel and truffle on GRAPES_PLUS.

Abroad: North Macedonia stands on the Oxford Companion entry and a general reference read through search; the small vineyards in Australia and China on Decanter and a trade page. The hosts could not be opened in this session.
TASTE gives body as medium minus (body 1); GRAPES_PLUS says medium and the entry follows the reviewed profile.

The Codex's Greek region records cite Wine Grapes with its three authors named in the title, and the Codex's Naoussa wine note calls Grande Reserve the Greek bottle most often set beside an old Barolo, a superlative; neither is this entry's to change, but a reviewer may wish to.
